fullText:
Fascinating paper from Google DeepMind.

They studied a market where AI agents bid to answer each user prompt.

Each agent bids its expected reward minus its inference cost. A first-price auction is simple to run, but bidders shade their bids, so a prompt can go to an agent that would not have produced the most value.

The paper shows two features of agent markets that keep this loss small. When several agents value a prompt close to the best one, for example because strong models are distilled into cheaper ones, competition limits the loss. When values mostly depend on how hard the prompt is, efficiency approaches 1 - 1/e^2 of optimal, well above the general bound of 1 - 1/e.

They find that simulations on the EmbedLLM routing dataset match the theory.

New work from Meta AI on agents that manage their own search.

(bookmark it)

A ReAct agent keeps every failed attempt in one context, making useful evidence harder to find.

To improve on this, they propose TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent’s own policy decides where to search.

In TreeFlex, the agent saves each intermediate state as a node in a search tree. The same model then reads short summaries of all nodes and decides where to continue, whether to branch, when to check a proposed answer, and when to stop.

On a deep-research benchmark, a 4B model reaches 48.8% versus 41.5% for flat ReAct, at the same context limit.

Same 9B base model, both trained with RL. 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified with TreeFlex, versus 43.3% with FoldAgent.

fullText:
Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. 

Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. 

So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context.

But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. 

Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. 

These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

// Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE agents //

It's standard practice to train SWE agents on binary test rewards.

This paper shows the problem with that. When every trajectory in a group passes, or every one fails, the reward has no contrast, and the group teaches nothing.

Researchers from Penn State and Microsoft Research propose Behavioral Self-Rewarding. The policy compares its own trajectories in pairs, and those preferences become small bounded rewards added on top of the test result.

The added rewards are bounded, so a self-judged preference can rank two passing trajectories but can never lift a failing one above a passing one.

No new environment interactions are needed. On SWE-bench Verified, Qwen3-14B improves from 32.1% to 34.7% average accuracy at a 400-step budget, and on SWE-bench-Live from 6.33% to 8.11%.

Banger paper from Stanford, Together AI, and colleagues.

Why is this an interesting paper?

Today's LLM agents must write out every reasoning step as text before they can search, run code, or take action.

Those steps cost tokens and can take time.

This paper proposes Hybrid Reasoning Agents, which reason internally in latent space and switch to text only to call a tool or give an answer.

A small module called HybridLink moves the model between the two modes, and a working memory keeps both kinds of context across turns. Tool calls stay in plain text, and the latent steps can still be inspected.

Training happens in two stages. SFT teaches the model to work with HybridLink, then RL teaches it when to think in latent space and when to act in text.

Across 11 benchmarks in math, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning, it outperforms frontier LLM agents and agentic frameworks, both text-based and latent, by 10.4% on average.

It also uses 35.5% to 54.7% fewer tokens, runs 1.8x to 2.6x faster, and costs 2.7x to 3.7x less.
